title: Thieboudienne with Tomato Sauce
localName: Thieboudienne — ceebu jen, poisson au riz
author: Imma Adamu
desc: The diaspora version built on tinned tomato sauce rather than a long paste reduction — the fish is fried three minutes a side first.
longDesc: A more tractable thieboudienne for a kitchen without a fishmonger: about three pounds of firm white fish, whole or bone-in steaks, marinated in a cup each of chopped parsley and basil and chopped green onions with five cloves of garlic. The fish is fried until brown, around three minutes, then two minutes on the other side. The sauce uses a fifteen-ounce tin of tomato sauce with two tablespoons of paste rather than two cups of paste, and eight ounces of smoked fish stands in for guedj. Three cups of rice, and the whole thing in under two hours.
ingredients: About 3 lb white, firm-fleshed fish, whole or bone-in steaks
2 lb mixed vegetables — carrots, green and red bell peppers, eggplant
3 cups uncooked short-grain rice — the author notes she used basmati
1 cup oil for frying the fish, plus 2 tbsp for the rice
steps: Blend the parsley and basil, green onions, garlic and optional habanero into a marinade.
Season the fish with the lemon, salt, white pepper, black pepper and bouillon powder, and stuff and coat it with the marinade.
Heat the cup of oil and fry the fish until brown, around 3 minutes, then brown it for two minutes on the other side. Set aside.
In the same pot soften the onion, then add the tomato sauce and tomato paste.
Let it cook for about 8 minutes.
Season, and let it simmer for about five minutes.
Add the smoked fish and cook for another 5 minutes.
Add the water or broth and bring to a simmer.
Add the potatoes and cassava and cook about 5 minutes, then the rest of the vegetables for about 3 minutes.
Return the fish, simmer until cooked through, then lift the fish and vegetables out and keep warm.
Add the rice to the broth with the 2 tablespoons of oil, cover and cook until tender and the liquid is absorbed.
Serve the rice with the fish and vegetables on top.
chefTips: Frying the fish first is the shortcut that makes this work — it firms the flesh so it survives the stew without the careful poaching the traditional method needs.
Three minutes then two. The uneven timing is deliberate: the first side gets the colour, the second just sets it.
A tin of tomato sauce plus two tablespoons of paste replaces two cups of paste cooked down. It is not the same depth, and the author is not pretending it is.
Smoked fish stands in for guedj here. It gives smoke rather than ferment, which is a real difference in the finished broth.
The author notes she used basmati despite calling for short-grain. Either works; basmati stays more separate.
Cook the vegetables in stages by density — potatoes and cassava first, the softer ones after.
If you want the traditional depth rather than the weeknight version, SEN001 is the long way round and worth the extra hour.
commonMistakes: Skipping the fry and poaching the fish instead, which this method's timings do not allow for.
All the vegetables in at once.
Expecting the fermented depth of a guedj-and-yeet version.
Too much broth left when the rice goes in.
sources: Adapted from 'Thieboudienne/Ceebu Jen (Poisson au Riz)', africanbites.com. BYLINE EXACTLY AS PRINTED: 'By Imma Adamu'. Published 7 December 2023, last updated 7 December 2023. Times as printed: Prep 35 minutes; Cook 1 hour 20 minutes; Total 1 hour 55 minutes. Yield as printed: 'Servings 8'.

SOURCING STATUS, stated precisely: TWO-PASS CORROBORATED BUT NOT VERBATIM. Both passes REFUSED strict verbatim transcription of the ingredient list and returned the quantities in paraphrase; the two paraphrases AGREE on every quantity. So the figures are twice-confirmed while the WORDING of the ingredient list above is the retrieval layer's, not the page's. That distinction is recorded rather than glossed over.

THE TIMES AND CUES, which pass two did supply as short verbatim fragments: 'fry until fish is brown, around 3 minutes'; 'brown it for two minutes on the other side'; 'Let it cook for about 8 minutes.' for the sauce; 'Let it simmer for about five minutes' after seasoning; then the smoked fish 'for another 5 minutes'; potatoes and cassava about 5 minutes, then the rest 'for about 3 minutes'.

A SUBSTITUTION THE READER SHOULD KNOW ABOUT: this version uses SMOKED fish where the traditional recipes use guedj, which is salted and FERMENTED as well as dried. Smoke is not ferment. The dish is good and the substitution is honest, but it is a different flavour from SEN001 and SEN002, not a convenience version of the same one.
AN INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY, recorded as printed: the ingredient list calls for short-grain rice while the author's own note says she used basmati.

WHY A THIRD CEEBU JEN IS PUBLISHED: the three documented versions represent three genuinely different approaches — a long tomato-paste reduction with guedj and yeet (SEN001), a fermented-seasoning-forward home version (SEN002), and a fried-fish, tinned-tomato diaspora version (this one). They are not duplicates of one recipe.
reheating: Steam the rice; warm the fish gently.
healthBenefits: High in protein from both fresh and smoked fish.
Four-plus pounds of vegetables across eight servings.
Tomato-led, so a good source of lycopene.
culturalNote: Senegalese cooking abroad runs into the guedj problem immediately — the fermented fish is hard to buy outside West African groceries, and smoked fish is what most diaspora kitchens reach for. This version is the honest result, and it is how a great many Senegalese households outside Senegal actually cook the national dish.
